Literal Interpretation

The War of the Kings

Genesis 14 opens with the first recorded war in Sacred Scripture, establishing the historical context of the ancient Near East during the time of the patriarchs. Four kings from the East—Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of nations—form an alliance and make war against five kings of the cities of the plain: the kings of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim, and Bela (Zoar). This coalition had been subject to Chedorlaomer for twelve years, paying tribute to the Elamite overlord, until they rebelled in the thirteenth year.

The battlefield was the Vale of Siddim, identified with the region of the Salt Sea (the Dead Sea). The five kings were defeated, and the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, falling into the slime pits (bitumen pits) that characterized the region. The victorious eastern alliance plundered Sodom and Gomorrah, taking captives including Lot, Abram's nephew, who had settled in Sodom.

St. Augustine, in his City of God (Book XVI), sets this narrative within the broader context of salvation history:

"When Abraham and Lot had separated, and dwelt apart, owing to the necessity of supporting their families, and not to vile discord, Abraham was in the land of Canaan, but Lot in Sodom. On the invasion of Sodom, when five kings carried on war against four, and Lot was taken captive with the conquered Sodomites, Abraham delivered him from the enemy, leading with him to battle three hundred and eighteen of his home-born servants."

St. Augustine, City of God, Book XVI, Chapter 22

Abram Rescues Lot

When a fugitive brought news of Lot's capture to Abram the Hebrew, who dwelt by the oaks of Mamre, Abram immediately mobilized his household forces. The text specifies that Abram armed three hundred and eighteen trained servants born in his house—a detail that demonstrates both Abram's considerable wealth and his capacity to mount a military expedition.

Abram pursued the four kings as far as Dan, divided his forces by night, and attacked, routing the enemy and pursuing them to Hobah, north of Damascus. He recovered all the goods, brought back Lot and his possessions, and also the women and the people. This swift, decisive military action reveals Abram not merely as a peaceful herdsman but as a capable commander willing to risk his life for his kinsman.

The Meeting with Melchizedek

Upon Abram's victorious return, he was met in the King's Valley by two figures: the king of Sodom and Melchizedek, king of Salem. Melchizedek's appearance is one of the most mysterious passages in Genesis. He is described as "priest of the most high God" (El Elyon)—the only individual called a priest in the Book of Genesis.

Melchizedek brought forth bread and wine and blessed Abram, saying: "Blessed be Abram by the most high God, who created heaven and earth. And blessed be the most high God, by whose protection the enemies are in thy hands" (Gen 14:19-20). In response, Abram gave Melchizedek a tenth of everything—the first recorded tithe in Scripture.

The name Melchizedek means "King of Righteousness," and Salem (traditionally identified with Jerusalem) means "Peace." He is thus king of righteousness and king of peace. St. Jerome notes the significance of his priesthood:

"Melchizedek offered not bloody victims, but dedicated the sacrament of Christ in bread and wine, a simple and pure sacrifice."

St. Jerome, Commentaries on the Gospel of Matthew

Abram Refuses the Spoils of Sodom

The king of Sodom offered Abram all the recovered goods, asking only for the return of the people. Abram firmly declined: "I lift up my hand to the Lord God the most high, the possessor of heaven and earth, that from the very woof thread unto the shoe latchet, I will not take of any things that are thine, lest thou say: I have enriched Abram" (Gen 14:22-23). Abram would accept nothing for himself, though he ensured his allies—Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre—received their portions.

This refusal demonstrates Abram's integrity and his determination that God alone should receive credit for his prosperity. He had sworn an oath to the Lord and would not compromise it, even when the spoils were legally his by right of conquest.

Historical and Geographical Notes

The chapter contains numerous geographical references that situate the narrative firmly in the ancient Near East. Shinar refers to Babylon; Elam was a powerful kingdom east of Mesopotamia; the route of the campaign follows a pattern consistent with known trade and military routes of the period. The place names and the pattern of eastern kings exacting tribute from Canaanite city-states reflect authentic features of second millennium BCE political arrangements.

Allegorical Interpretation

The 318 Servants and the Cross of Christ

The Church Fathers discovered profound Christological meaning in the number of Abram's servants: three hundred and eighteen. This interpretation, found as early as the Epistle of Barnabas (c. 70-135 AD), employs Greek gematria (numerical values of letters) to reveal Christ hidden in the Old Testament narrative.

The Epistle of Barnabas explains:

"Mark, first the eighteen, and next the three hundred. For the numeral letters of ten and eight are I H [Iota and Eta]. And these denote Jesus. And because the cross was that by which we were to find grace; therefore he adds, three hundred; the note of which is T (the figure of his cross). Wherefore by two letters he signified Jesus, and by the third his cross."

Epistle of Barnabas, 9:8

In Greek numerical notation, 300 is represented by the letter Tau (T), which resembles a cross; 10 is Iota (I) and 8 is Eta (H)—together IH, the first two letters of IHSOYS (Jesus). Thus Abram conquers with 318 servants, and Christians conquer through Jesus and His Cross. St. Clement of Alexandria affirms this reading:

"For, hearing that Lot was taken captive, having numbered his own servants, born in his house, 318, he defeats a very great number of the enemy. They say, then, that the character representing 300 is, as to shape, the type of the Lord's sign, and that the Iota and the Eta indicate the Saviour's name."

Clement of Alexandria, Stromata

It is notable that the First Council of Nicaea (325 AD), which definitively condemned Arianism and proclaimed the divinity of Christ, was attended by 318 bishops—a number the Church has seen as providentially significant, connecting the Fathers' defense of Christ's divinity to Abram's victory.

Melchizedek as Type of Christ

The figure of Melchizedek is the richest typological treasure of Genesis 14. The Epistle to the Hebrews (chapters 5-7) develops at length how Melchizedek prefigures Christ, and the Church Fathers unanimously follow this interpretation.

St. John Chrysostom draws the connection explicitly:

"Melchizedek was righteous and the faithful image of Christ. Moved by a prophetic spirit, he discerned the oblation which must one day be offered for the Gentiles, and, in the example of the future Christ, he offered bread and wine as sacrifice to God."

St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Hebrews

Several parallels establish Melchizedek as a type of Christ:

  • King of Righteousness: Melchizedek's name means "king of righteousness"; Christ is "Jesus Christ the righteous" (1 Jn 2:1) and the source of all righteousness.
  • King of Salem (Peace): Christ is the "Prince of Peace" (Is 9:6), who brings peace between God and man.
  • Priest of the Most High God: Christ is our eternal High Priest, offering Himself as the perfect sacrifice.
  • Without Genealogy: Hebrews notes that Melchizedek appears "without father, without mother, without genealogy" in the narrative—foreshadowing the eternal priesthood of Christ, who has no beginning or end.

The Bread and Wine and the Eucharist

The bread and wine brought forth by Melchizedek constitute the most significant typological element. The Fathers consistently interpreted this offering as a prefiguration of the Eucharist. St. Cyprian of Carthage states directly:

"In the priest Melchizedek we see prefigured the sacrament of the sacrifice of the Lord, according to what divine Scripture testifies: 'And Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought forth bread and wine.' He was a priest of the most high God, and blessed Abraham."

St. Cyprian, Epistle to Caecilius on the Sacrament of the Cup of the Lord

St. Jerome emphasizes the contrast with Levitical sacrifice:

"Just as Melchizedek, the priest of the Most High God, in prefiguring Him, made bread and wine an offering, He too makes Himself manifest in the reality of His own Body and Blood."

St. Jerome, Commentaries on the Gospel of Matthew

St. Ambrose draws a profound conclusion about the antiquity of Christian worship:

"The Christian worship is more ancient than that of the Law, since it is Melchizedek, the image of Christ, who brings the bread and the wine, not Abraham. The priesthood and the sacrifice are a duty of the human condition; for like a lamb He was led to the slaughter, and He is a priest according to the order of Melchizedek."

St. Ambrose, De Sacramentis, IV, 8, 10-11

St. Chrysostom contrasts this with Aaronic sacrifice:

"The Judaic synagogue, which honored God according to the order of Aaron, offered Him a sacrifice, not of bread and wine, but of bulls and lambs and glorified the Lord by bloody sacrifices. That is why God, addressing Himself to the One Who was to be born of the Virgin Mary, Jesus Christ, His Son, says to Him, 'You are Priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek' and not according to the order of Aaron."

St. John Chrysostom, Homilies

Abram as Figure of Christ the Redeemer

Abram's rescue of Lot from captivity prefigures Christ's redemption of humanity from the bondage of sin and death. As Lot was taken captive through his association with sinful Sodom, so humanity was taken captive through Adam's sin. As Abram left his place of safety and pursued the enemy to deliver his kinsman, so Christ left the glory of heaven, entered the domain of the enemy, and conquered sin, death, and the devil to rescue His people.

The title "kinsman-redeemer" (go'el), though not used explicitly in this passage, describes Abram's action. Christ is the ultimate Kinsman-Redeemer who, by taking on our human nature, became our near kinsman and thus qualified to redeem us from bondage.

The Two Kings: Righteousness and Wickedness

Abram's encounter with two kings upon his return—Melchizedek and the king of Sodom—represents the two spiritual kingdoms between which every soul must choose. Melchizedek offers bread and wine, blessing and communion with God; the king of Sodom offers material wealth and entanglement with the world. Abram receives the blessing of Melchizedek and refuses the gifts of Sodom—choosing the kingdom of God over the kingdom of this world.

Moral (Tropological) Interpretation

The Virtue of Fraternal Charity

When Abram heard that Lot had been taken captive, he did not hesitate. Though Lot had chosen the well-watered plain of Jordan and left Abram with less desirable territory (Genesis 13), Abram bore no grudge. He immediately armed his servants and set out to rescue his kinsman. This exemplifies the duty of charity toward family and neighbor, especially in times of distress.

The moral lesson is clear: past disagreements or perceived slights must not prevent us from coming to the aid of those in need. Christian charity requires that we forget offenses and respond generously when others are in trouble. As St. Ambrose teaches regarding Abraham's character:

"We have spoken daily upon subjects connected with morals, when the deeds of the Patriarchs or the precepts of the Proverbs were being read, in order that being taught and instructed by these you might grow accustomed to enter the ways of the ancients and to walk in their paths."

St. Ambrose, On the Mysteries

Courage as a Christian Virtue

Genesis 14 reveals a different aspect of Abram's character than the preceding chapters. In Genesis 13, we see his meekness and willingness to yield his rights for the sake of peace. Here we see his courage and decisive action in the face of danger. Both are essential virtues in the Christian life.

The moral tradition notes:

"We generally associate godliness with the passive rather than the active virtues, but in view of Hebrews 11 we must not forget the two sides of the Christian life. In Genesis 13, Abraham is seen manifesting the passive virtues of unselfishness, humility, and willingness to yield his rights. In chapter 14, however, there is all the decision and initiative of the brave and fearless man. Courage is as real a Christian virtue as humility."

Traditional moral commentary

Abram did not count the cost or calculate the odds. Four kings with their armies had defeated five kings—yet Abram pursued them with only 318 men. Such courage flows from faith in God's providence and protection.

Humility in Victory

Having won a remarkable military victory, Abram showed no pride or self-glorification. He attributed the victory entirely to God. When Melchizedek blessed him, saying "Blessed be the most high God, by whose protection the enemies are in thy hands" (Gen 14:20), Abram agreed wholeheartedly—demonstrated by his giving a tenth of everything to God's priest.

St. Ambrose draws the moral lesson:

"One who is victorious should not claim the victory for himself; rather, he should attribute it to God. This is the teaching of Abraham, who became more humble, not more proud, in victory. Indeed, he offered a sacrifice and gave tithes; for this reason too, he received the blessing of Melchizedek."

St. Ambrose, On Abraham

The proud heart claims credit for its achievements; the humble heart recognizes that every good gift comes from God. Abram's tithe was an act of worship and acknowledgment that God alone deserved the glory for his victory.

Detachment from Worldly Wealth

Abram's refusal of the king of Sodom's offer demonstrates the virtue of detachment from material goods. He would not take "from the very woof thread unto the shoe latchet" (Gen 14:23) lest anyone say that the king of Sodom had made Abram rich. His prosperity must come from God alone.

This refusal teaches several moral lessons:

  • Integrity: Abram would not be beholden to the wicked king of Sodom or entangled in obligations to him.
  • Trust in God: Abram trusted God to provide for him rather than accepting wealth from human sources that might compromise his witness.
  • Protection of Reputation: He guarded his testimony, ensuring no one could attribute his blessings to anything other than God's favor.

The Duty of Tithing

Abram's tithe to Melchizedek establishes the principle of giving a tenth to God's service. Though this predates the Mosaic Law, it demonstrates that the faithful have always recognized the obligation to return a portion of their blessings to God. The tithe expresses gratitude, acknowledges God's ownership of all things, and supports those who minister in sacred service.

Considering the Needs of Others

While Abram refused the spoils for himself, he ensured that his allies—Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre—received their fair portion: "Saving only what the young men have eaten, and the shares of the men that came with me, Aner, Eshcol, and Mambre: these shall take their shares" (Gen 14:24). This demonstrates the virtue of justice: Abram would not impose his own scruples upon others who had risked their lives in battle, nor would he deny them what was rightfully theirs.

The Blessing of the Righteous

Melchizedek blessed Abram, and Abram received the blessing with reverence. This teaches us to value spiritual blessings above material goods. Abram could have had great wealth from Sodom; instead, he received the blessing of God's priest. The blessing of the righteous is worth more than all the treasures of the wicked.

The Mystery of Providence

St. Augustine's reflection on this chapter reminds us of God's providence working through human events:

"Abraham was then openly blessed by Melchizedek, who was priest of God most high, about whom many and great things are written in the epistle that is inscribed to the Hebrews."

St. Augustine, City of God, Book XVI

What seemed like a calamity—Lot's capture—became the occasion for Abram to demonstrate faith, courage, and generosity, and to receive the blessing that pointed toward Christ. So too in our lives, apparent disasters may become opportunities for virtue and vessels of divine grace.

Anagogical Interpretation

Melchizedek and the Eternal Priesthood

The anagogical sense directs our gaze from earthly realities to heavenly fulfillment. Melchizedek, appearing mysteriously without recorded genealogy, "without father, without mother, without descent, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like unto the Son of God" (Heb 7:3), points to the eternal priesthood of Christ in heaven.

The Epistle to the Hebrews develops this at length: Christ, risen and ascended, exercises His priesthood forever in the heavenly sanctuary. Unlike the Levitical priests who served in an earthly copy of the true tabernacle and who died and were replaced, Christ "continueth forever, hath an everlasting priesthood" (Heb 7:24). The earthly priesthood of Melchizedek foreshadows this eternal heavenly ministry.

Salem and the Heavenly Jerusalem

Melchizedek was king of Salem, identified by tradition with Jerusalem. But Salem also means "Peace," and this priest-king of peace reigning in Salem points toward the heavenly Jerusalem, where Christ reigns as eternal King of Righteousness and Prince of Peace.

The Epistle to the Hebrews declares: "But you are come to mount Sion, and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem" (Heb 12:22). As Melchizedek was king of the earthly Salem, Christ is King of the heavenly Jerusalem, where the blessed will dwell forever in perfect peace.

St. John's vision in Revelation describes this eternal city: "And I John saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband" (Rev 21:2). The encounter at Salem anticipates the eternal communion of the saints with Christ in the city of God.

The Eucharistic Banquet and the Marriage Supper of the Lamb

The bread and wine offered by Melchizedek, while prefiguring the Eucharist in its sacramental sense, points ultimately to the eschatological banquet—the Marriage Supper of the Lamb. The Eucharist is the foretaste of heaven, the pledge of future glory.

St. John Chrysostom emphasizes the continuity between the earthly and heavenly liturgy:

"This Sacrifice, no matter who offers it, be it Peter or Paul, is always the same as that which Christ gave His disciples and which priests now offer: The offering of today is in no way inferior to that which Christ offered, because it is not men who sanctify the offering of today; it is the same Christ who sanctified His own."

St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Second Timothy

The earthly Eucharist participates in the eternal offering of Christ before the Father's throne. In heaven, the sacramental signs will give way to the reality itself—perfect communion with God, the eternal feast that satisfies every hunger.

Victory Over the Powers of Darkness

Abram's military victory over the four kings foreshadows Christ's definitive victory over the powers of darkness. As Abram defeated the kings who had taken Lot captive, Christ has defeated sin, death, and the devil who held humanity in bondage. This victory, accomplished on the Cross and manifested in the Resurrection, will be fully revealed at the Second Coming.

The four kings represent the forces of this world—political power, violence, oppression—that stand against God's people. Abram's triumph with his 318 servants, bearing the sign of Jesus and His Cross in their very number, anticipates the final triumph when every knee shall bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord.

The Rescue of the Captives

Lot's rescue from captivity prefigures the ultimate liberation of souls from the prison of death and hell. Christ, in His descent to the dead, led captivity captive and brought forth the righteous souls who awaited redemption. At the general resurrection, all the dead will be brought forth—some to eternal life, some to eternal judgment.

The anagogical hope is liberation from every bondage: the freedom of the children of God in the glorious liberty of the new creation, where there will be no more captivity, no more oppression, no more exile from the presence of God.

The Tithe and Eternal Reward

Abram's tithe to Melchizedek represents the offering of our lives and labors to God, which will be rewarded in eternity. "Lay up to yourselves treasures in heaven: where neither the rust nor moth doth consume, and where thieves do not break through, nor steal" (Mt 6:20). What we give to God in this life we receive back multiplied in glory.

The Refusal of Sodom's Wealth

Abram's refusal of the spoils of Sodom teaches the soul to set its hope not on the passing treasures of this world but on the eternal inheritance. Sodom was soon to be destroyed by fire from heaven (Genesis 19)—all its wealth reduced to ashes. Those who cling to the goods of this world will see them perish. Those who, like Abram, refuse the world's wealth in favor of God's blessing will possess an inheritance that cannot fade or perish.

The Blessing of the Most High God

Melchizedek's blessing, "Blessed be Abram by the most high God, who created heaven and earth" (Gen 14:19), anticipates the eternal blessing pronounced upon the righteous at the Last Judgment: "Come, ye blessed of my Father, possess you the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world" (Mt 25:34).

The "most high God, who created heaven and earth" is the God who will create the new heaven and new earth, where righteousness dwells. The blessing Abram received from Melchizedek finds its ultimate fulfillment in the beatific vision—seeing God face to face in the eternal kingdom, where the blessed will reign with Christ forever as kings and priests unto God.

St. Augustine reflects on the eschatological dimension:

"He was then openly blessed by Melchizedek, who was priest of God most high, about whom many and great things are written in the epistle that is inscribed to the Hebrews, which most have attributed to the Apostle Paul. Then first appeared the sacrifice which is now offered to God by Christians in the whole wide world."

St. Augustine, City of God, Book XVI

This sacrifice, offered first in figure by Melchizedek, continues in the Eucharist, and will reach its consummation in the eternal worship of heaven, where the Lamb who was slain receives glory and honor and blessing forever and ever.
